Predicting the grid draw, then flattening it

A 1 GW campus frees a whole data center's worth of grid power

Flattening cut your twin's billed peak by 12.5% while delivering nearly the same work. Scaled linearly, with the battery sized in the same ratio (0.35 MWh per 4.2 MW):

FacilityDemand-charge savings / yrPeak grid power freedHomes’ worth of powerNew build avoided at $11.3M/MW

Savings range: 0.35 MWh-ratio battery to 2 MWh-ratio battery. Homes use the US average of 10,791 kWh a year (1.23 kW average draw). On a 1 GW campus the freed 125 MW is about one typical AI data center: the IEA puts one at the electricity use of 100,000 households. Build cost is JLL's 2026 global average. The freed peak lets that much more compute run on the same grid connection without a new interconnection.

MW is power: how hard the site is pulling from the grid at each instant. MWh is energy, power × time: a battery's size, or energy used. The utility bills both: a demand charge on the peak MW and an energy charge on the MWh.

1 · The predictor

Three layers, trained on six other twin days

  1. Scheduler layer (minutes to hours). Uses what the scheduler knows at that moment: running jobs and their node counts, requested walltimes, the queue, and its own FIFO rule. It replays the queue forward and blends toward an hour-of-day prior for jobs that haven't arrived yet. Busy nodes × learned power per node (~3.4 kW) + idle nodes × 0.46 kW gives hall IT load in MW.
  2. Oscillation layer (1–60 s). An AR(40) model on the residual (measured minus scheduler layer), refit every 5 min, carries the training-step swing forward. Your traces swing at about 0.094 Hz, ±0.11 MW at the busiest hour.
  3. Facility layer. A regression from forecast IT load, forecast ambient (±1 °C error) and the current cooling state to site draw at the 13.8 kV feed. It is fit on twin days with seeds 11–16 and tested on your seed-7 day, so nothing from the test day leaks in.
2 · Distributing the load

What actually moves the bill

  • Power-aware scheduler. This keeps your twin's FIFO scheduler and adds one rule: a job starts only if busy nodes stay at or below 85% of the cluster (921 nodes). Because the predictor turns busy nodes into kW, that is a power cap of about 2.96 MW at the meter. It also ramps jobs in over 120 s and down over 60 s, and starts each job at the phase offset (0–13 s) that best cancels the jobs already running.
  • Battery. The hold battery from the one-line: 1 MW of power, 0.35 MWh of stored energy (about 20 minutes at full output). It always smooths: the grid follows a 2-minute mean of the predicted draw. It also shaves to a cap while charge stays above 35%. With the scheduler, that cap comes from the node cap minus what the battery can cover over a 2 h plateau. Without the scheduler, it comes from the 4 h-ahead forecast. If the cap turns out too low, it is raised to the current draw, because once a peak is set it already counts for the month.

Scenarios except the first are run with faults off, against a fault-free as-is run of the same seed. Phase interleaving and soft ramps hardly change the bill: your traces drift out of phase within minutes, and ramps only soften job edges. A battery alone smooths the 1 s signal almost completely but can't lower the 30-min peak on this day. Without a forecast, its recharging raises the peak. “Perfect cap” means the lowest cap the battery could have held if it knew the whole day.

4 · Reading the money

The scheduler does most of the work

The node cap alone is worth $69k/yr, and adding the 0.35 MWh battery that's already on the one-line takes it to $89k. Against an energy bill of about $1.4 M a year that's 6%. The price is queue time: mean wait goes from 24 to 104 min at an 85% cap.

The battery's main contribution is power quality, not the bill. The day's 1 s jumps over 0.2 MW drop from 8,019 to 0, the training-step swing from 0.17 to 0.01 MW, and LV bus peak loading from 86% to 66%. That headroom lets the same electrical gear host more nodes, and it's what interconnection ramp limits care about. This tariff doesn't price either.

Assumptions
  • Your twin's limits carry over: one workload (Llama-2 70B LoRA), jobs above 16 nodes built from 16-node traces, nodes in lockstep (sync jitter 0), an invented job mix, and a proposed cooling plant.
  • The twin has no requested walltimes, so the scheduler layer assumes users ask for 1.0–1.6× the true runtime. The battery's smoothing target assumes job-end telemetry accurate to about 20 s.
  • The battery is applied at the meter on top of the twin's site draw, not inside the DC bus model.
  • Demand rate $19,400 per MW-month ($19.40/kW): Dominion GS-4 primary on-peak generation, transmission and distribution demand plus riders T1, GEN, CE, E and SNA (2025 filings), on the monthly 30-min peak. One simulated day stands in for the month's worst day. Across the six training days, as-is site peaks ran 3.8–3.9 MW, so the month's billed peak is likely somewhat higher than this day's.
  • Scaling assumes a bigger site has the same load shape. A larger campus runs more jobs at once, which smooths its draw on its own, so the true percentage may be smaller. The node cap shifted about 2.5% of the day's node-hours into the next day.
  • The scheduler scenarios use a Python mirror of dctwin_itload_traces.m driven by the twin's job table. It matches your CSV's IT load to within 0.005 kW at every second.
